title: The Protocol of Tashkent
premise: Tamsin Quintana, a disgraced intelligence analyst fired from three agencies for asking the wrong questions, receives a voiceprint authentication that matches their own voice — recorded before they ever spoke. The voiceprint unlocks a server in Tashkent containing 'The Protocol,' a tri-government black site program that erases and rewrites witnesses' memories to bury a massacre both Uzbekistan, Britain, and the US agreed never happened. Hunted by an assassin who is herself a Protocol subject with fragmented recall of her own crimes, Tamsin races across Central Asia with a defected archivist who may be their forgotten sibling. In the end Tamsin gets the archive to a journalist as dawn breaks over the extraction airfield, choosing exile and truth over reinstatement — while the assassin, given her real name back, lets them board.
about_author: Noor Oyelaran is a former policy researcher who spent four years in Central Asia documenting border archives before turning to fiction. They write thrillers about people trapped between institutions that would rather erase them than answer them.

chapters.title: The Voice That Wasn't Mine
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Five years after being pushed out of GCHQ, Tamsin runs compliance audits in London until a dead colleague's voiceprint — spliced with Tamsin's own voice — unlocks an encrypted drop naming Tashkent. The emotional beat: dread recognition that someone has been keeping a file on them all along.

chapters.title: Compliance Is a Kind of Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, flashback-woven. We learn why three agencies discarded them: each time they flagged anomalies around a 2019 Fergana Valley operation, the rules changed overnight. Their old handler offers quiet reinstatement if they drop it. Beat: the ache of belonging offered at the price of forgetting.

chapters.title: Layover in a City of Mirrors
chapters.summary: Tamsin flies to Tashkent under a consultant cover and meets Dilnoza Rakhimova, a state archivist who claims she built the server's index — and who recognizes Tamsin's face from a file she was ordered to shred. Beat: wary alliance; two people who survive by noticing what others are told not to see.

chapters.title: The Server Under the Madrasa
chapters.summary: Dilnoza's POV. She leads Tamsin through Old Town to a cold-storage node hidden behind a restored madrasa wall. Inside: thousands of memory-erasure consent forms, all signed by people officially listed as dead. Beat: vertigo — the scale of the Protocol made physical.

chapters.title: Three Flags, One Grave
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Cross-referencing files reveals Operation KARAVAN: a joint UK-US-Uzbek raid that killed civilians, then laundered the event by wiping every witness who saw it. Tamsin realizes their own termination orders trace back to it. Beat: cold fury replacing self-doubt.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Forgets on Purpose
chapters.summary: Assassin Yulduz's POV, first appearance. A Protocol-trained cleaner arrives in Tashkent with a mission brief she cannot fully read — her own memory was edited after each job. She finds the madrasa node already burned. Beat: eerie sympathy; the hunter is also a victim who doesn't know it yet.

chapters.title: Burn Notice, Burned Building
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The node is torched minutes after they leave; Dilnoza's apartment is searched. They flee toward Samarkand on a night train with a copied drive hidden in a Koran stand. Beat: paranoia sharpening into resolve; trust becomes survival equipment.

chapters.title: What the Train Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. On the train, Dilnoza reveals the drive contains biometric templates — including one matching Tamsin's DNA profile logged years before Tamsin entered any agency. Beat: identity destabilized; Tamsin begins suspecting they were inside the Protocol once.

chapters.title: Samarkand, After Hours
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A retired CIA linguist, Marat Cole, agrees to decrypt the templates but warns that three governments have quietly agreed the Protocol must stay buried — cooperation, not rivalry, is the enemy. Beat: the walls closing in feel institutional, not personal.

chapters.title: Yulduz Closes the Circle
chapters.summary: Yulduz's POV. She tracks them to Samarkand but hesitates when she sees Tamsin's face triggers a flash of her own erased past — a hospital corridor, a child's hand. Beat: fracture in the assassin's conditioning; mercy as malfunction.

chapters.title: The Archive of Names
chapters.summary: Dilnoza's POV. Decryption completes: among the wiped subjects is 'A. Quintana.' Tamsin confronts the possibility that Dilnoza — whose childhood records were also purged — is their sister, separated during the same operation. Beat: grief and hope colliding mid-escape.

chapters.title: Rooftops of Registan
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Yulduz corners them atop a medressa; instead of killing them, she demands the file on herself. Tamsin gives her a copy. Gunshots from government minders force all three to flee together. Beat: enemies become reluctant convoy.

chapters.title: The Road to Nukus
chapters.summary: Travel chapter, rotating POV. The trio drives toward the Aral Sea where a decommissioned airfield hosts the dawn extraction flight Tamsin can still summon via old favors. Beat: exhausted intimacy; three broken people building a temporary country of their own.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Firelight
chapters.summary: Yulduz's POV. At a roadside stop, Yulduz reads her own file: she was the child witness from Fergana, wiped and weaponized. She tells Tamsin what she remembers of the massacre — testimony no living official will confirm. Beat: the price of survival made explicit; memory returned as wound.

chapters.title: London Calls Collect
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The old handler reaches them via satellite phone: full reinstatement, pensions restored, everything forgiven — if the drive dies here. Tamsin hears, for the first time, genuine fear in the man's voice. Beat: temptation reframed as threat; belonging exposed as leash.

chapters.title: The Deal at the Dry Dock
chapters.summary: Dilnoza's POV. A moored rusting freighter near Moynaq becomes a dead-drop point for a Guardian correspondent. But the meet is compromised — Marat Cole sold the route. Beat: betrayal; the trio scatters under fire, drive nearly lost.

chapters.title: Salt and Static
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Wounded, separated from Dilnoza, Tamsin crosses the salt flats toward the airfield carrying the only remaining copy, guided by Yulduz who now knows the terrain from her erased childhood. Beat: endurance stripped to essentials; the desert as memory itself.

chapters.title: What Dilnoza Chose
chapters.summary: Dilnoza's POV. Captured by Uzbek security services, Dilnoza stalls her interrogators by reciting names from the archive aloud, buying Tamsin hours while refusing to give up the flight time. Beat: sacrifice; the archivist becomes the archive.

chapters.title: Runway Zero-Four
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Pre-dawn at the abandoned airfield: the extraction plane descends, government forces converge, and Yulduz holds the perimeter, finally fighting against her handlers. Beat: climax ignition; every debt comes due at once.

chapters.title: The Truth Gets Boarding Priority
chapters.summary: Climax, Tamsin's POV. Under fire, Tamsin uploads the entire Protocol archive to the journalist mid-runway and broadcasts the verification hash publicly so it cannot be quietly killed. The handler's voice on the radio offers one last deal; Tamsin answers by stepping onto the plane. Beat: choice crystallized — truth over belonging.

chapters.title: Extraction
chapters.summary: Yulduz's POV. Wounded, Yulduz watches the plane lift into the sunrise and walks away from her handlers, carrying her recovered name like contraband. Dilnoza's fate is unknown; the last image is her interrogation room door opening. Beat: costly victory; survival without absolution.

chapters.title: The Protocol of Tashkent
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Tamsin's POV, six months later. From exile in Montevideo, Tamsin watches the hearings begin as governments deny everything while quietly retiring the Program. A postcard arrives from Tashkent — Dilnoza's handwriting, one word: 'Sister?' Beat: bittersweet resolution; memory endures even when justice doesn't.
